cards.prompt: sales_gaps has some missing revenue values. Select just the rows where revenue is missing. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: isna() produces a boolean mask marking every missing (NaN) value, which can filter rows like any other condition.
cards.whenToUse: Inspecting exactly which rows have a gap before deciding how to handle it.
cards.commonMistake: Comparing to None or NaN with ==, which never matches — NaN isn't equal to anything, including itself.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 1   East    Shoes      NaN      9
# 5   East    Shoes      NaN      7

cards.prompt: Select just the rows where revenue is NOT missing. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: notna() is the exact inverse of isna() — True wherever a value is present.
cards.whenToUse: Working only with the complete, known values in a column.
cards.commonMistake: Writing ~sales_gaps['revenue'].isna() instead — correct, but notna() says the same thing more directly.
cards.example: # 6 rows — every row except the two with missing revenue

cards.prompt: Count how many missing values each column has. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: isna() turns every cell into True/False, and sum() treats True as 1, giving a per-column missing-value count.
cards.whenToUse: A first-pass audit of how much data is missing, column by column.
cards.commonMistake: Calling .count() instead, which counts non-null values, the opposite of what's being asked here.

cards.prompt: Drop every row that has at least one missing value, in any column.
cards.why: dropna() defaults to how='any' — a row is dropped the moment a single column is missing.
cards.whenToUse: You need a fully complete DataFrame and can afford to lose partially-filled rows.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming dropna() only checks one specific column — by default it checks every column.
cards.example: # 4 rows remain — every row with a gap in any column is gone

cards.prompt: Drop rows only where revenue specifically is missing — ignore gaps in any other column. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: subset restricts which columns are checked for missing values, instead of the default 'any column'.
cards.whenToUse: One particular column is required, but gaps elsewhere are fine to keep.
cards.commonMistake: Calling plain dropna() here, which would also drop rows whose only gap is in a different column.
cards.example: # 6 rows remain — only the 2 rows with missing revenue are dropped

cards.prompt: Drop a row only if every single value in it is missing, not just one. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: how='all' requires every column in a row to be NaN before it's dropped, a much stricter bar than the default how='any'.
cards.whenToUse: Filtering out completely blank rows (e.g. from a bad CSV export) while keeping partially-filled ones.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming how='all' behaves like the default — it keeps far more rows, since a real dataset rarely has every column missing at once.
cards.example: # all 8 rows remain — no row here is completely empty

cards.prompt: Keep only rows that have at least 3 non-missing values out of the 4 columns. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: thresh sets a minimum number of non-null values a row must have to survive, a middle ground between how='any' and how='all'.
cards.whenToUse: Rows with one small gap are still useful, but rows missing most of their data aren't.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing thresh's meaning with how='all' — thresh counts required non-null values, not required null values.
cards.example: # 7 rows remain — only the row missing both category and units is dropped

cards.prompt: Fill missing revenue values with 0. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: fillna() replaces every NaN in a Series or DataFrame with the given value.
cards.whenToUse: Missing genuinely means 'none', e.g. no sales recorded.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting fillna() returns a new Series — sales_gaps itself is unchanged unless reassigned or inplace=True is passed.

cards.prompt: Fill missing revenue values with the column's own average, instead of a fixed number. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: mean() automatically skips NaNs when computing the average, so it's safe to feed straight back into fillna().
cards.whenToUse: A reasonable default value beats zero when zero would misrepresent a plausible sale.
cards.commonMistake: Computing the mean on a column that still contains the missing values being filled — mean() already ignores NaN by default, so this isn't actually a problem, but it's worth knowing why.

cards.prompt: Forward-fill missing revenue values using the previous valid value. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: ffill() carries the last known value forward into each following gap.
cards.whenToUse: Time-ordered data where a missing reading likely equals the last known one.
cards.commonMistake: Using the older fillna(method='ffill') spelling — the direct .ffill() method is the current, non-deprecated way to write this.

cards.prompt: Backward-fill missing revenue values using the next valid value instead. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: bfill() is the mirror of ffill() — it looks forward to the next known value instead of back.
cards.whenToUse: The next reading is a better estimate for a gap than the previous one.
cards.commonMistake: Mixing up ffill and bfill — one looks backward in the sequence, the other forward.

cards.prompt: Fill missing revenue with 0 and missing units with 1, in a single call.
cards.why: Passing a dict lets each column get its own fill value in one call, instead of filling column by column.
cards.whenToUse: Different columns need different, column-appropriate defaults.
cards.commonMistake: Calling fillna(0) on the whole DataFrame, which forces every column to the same fill value.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 1   East    Shoes      0.0    9.0
# 4   West     None     45.0    1.0

cards.prompt: Fill missing revenue values using linear interpolation between the surrounding known values, instead of a fixed fill. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: interpolate() estimates each gap as a straight line between its nearest known neighbors, rather than one flat value for every gap.
cards.whenToUse: Roughly continuous data (like a running total or a sensor reading) where a straight-line estimate beats a constant.
cards.commonMistake: Using interpolate() on unordered or categorical data, where 'between' has no real meaning.

cards.prompt: Fill missing revenue values with 0. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: fillna() replaces every NaN in the Series with the given value.
cards.commonMistake: Passing the string '0' instead of the number 0, which fills with text rather than a usable number.

cards.prompt: Which call correctly returns the TOTAL number of missing values across the whole DataFrame, as a single number?
cards.why: The first sum() gives a per-column count (a Series); the second sum() adds those column counts into one grand total.
cards.whenToUse: A single headline number for 'how much data is missing overall.'
cards.commonMistake: Stopping after one sum(), which gives a per-column breakdown instead of a single overall total.
